questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Personal protective equipment worn in a woodwork shop, such as goggles and dust masks, is primarily intended to
options: reduce the cost of workshop tools
protect the worker from wood dust, flying chips, and other hazards
increase the speed at which tasks are completed
questions.explanation: PPE such as goggles and dust masks shields woodwork students and craftsmen from flying chips, sawdust, and other airborne hazards.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A key safety practice when using sharp hand tools such as chisels is to always
options: use a blunt chisel to reduce risk
leave sharp tools scattered on the workbench
cut toward the body for better control
cut away from the body, keeping hands behind the cutting edge
questions.explanation: Cutting away from the body and keeping hands behind the cutting edge reduces the risk of serious injury if the tool slips.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A key safety measure when operating high-speed woodworking machinery, such as a circular saw, is to
options: operate the machine without any training
remove all safety guards for better visibility
ensure guards are in place and never bypass safety interlocks
questions.explanation: Machine guards and safety interlocks are critical protections against contact with fast-moving blades and should never be bypassed.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The first-aid treatment generally recommended for a minor splinter injury is to
options: carefully remove the splinter with sterilised tweezers and clean the wound
ignore the injury and continue working
apply wood glue over the wound
leave the splinter in place indefinitely
questions.explanation: Minor splinters should be carefully removed with sterilised tweezers, followed by cleaning the wound to prevent infection.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A tool used to measure and check straight lengths in a woodwork shop is called a
questions.explanation: A rule is a basic graduated measuring tool used to measure straight lengths of timber and components.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A tool used to check or mark an accurate 90-degree angle between two surfaces of a workpiece is called a
questions.explanation: A try square provides a fixed 90-degree reference, used to check squareness or mark right angles on timber.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A tool used to check or mark a 45-degree angle, commonly used for mitred corner joints, is called a
questions.explanation: A mitre square is fixed at 45 degrees, used specifically for marking and checking mitred joints in woodwork.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A tool with an adjustable blade, used to mark or check angles other than 90 or 45 degrees, is called a
questions.explanation: A sliding bevel has an adjustable blade, allowing it to mark or check any angle, unlike the fixed angles of a try square or mitre square.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A tool used to scribe a line parallel to the edge of a piece of timber, using a single spur or pin, is called a
questions.explanation: A marking gauge uses a single scribing pin to mark a line at a set distance parallel to an edge, useful for marking out joints.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A tool similar to a marking gauge, but with two adjustable spurs, used specifically to mark the two parallel lines of a mortise or tenon is called a
questions.explanation: A mortise gauge has two adjustable pins, allowing both sides of a mortise or tenon to be marked simultaneously and accurately.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A saw with widely spaced, chisel-like teeth, designed specifically for cutting along the grain of timber, is called a
questions.explanation: A ripsaw has teeth shaped like small chisels, designed to efficiently cut along (with) the grain of timber.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A saw with teeth shaped like small knives, designed specifically for cutting across the grain of timber, is called a
questions.explanation: A crosscut saw's teeth are angled and shaped to slice cleanly across (against) the grain of timber.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A general-purpose handsaw with fine teeth suitable for both ripping and crosscutting on thinner stock is called a
questions.explanation: A panel saw is a versatile, finer-toothed handsaw suited to cutting panels and thinner timber sections.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A backed saw with fine teeth, used for accurate cutting of joints such as tenons, is called a
questions.explanation: A tenon saw has a rigid metal back for stability and fine teeth, ideal for the precise cuts needed in joinery such as tenons.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A small, fine-toothed backed saw specifically used for cutting the narrow slots of dovetail joints is called a
questions.explanation: A dovetail saw is a small, fine-toothed backed saw designed for the precise, narrow cuts required in dovetail joinery.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A saw with a thin, narrow blade held in a frame, used to cut curves and intricate shapes in timber, is called a
questions.explanation: A coping saw's thin blade, mounted in a frame, allows it to follow curved lines and cut intricate internal shapes.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A hand plane used for the initial rough removal of material from timber surfaces is called a
questions.explanation: The jack plane is a general-purpose plane commonly used for the initial, rougher shaping and levelling of timber surfaces.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A hand plane used to produce a fine, smooth final finish on a timber surface is called a
questions.explanation: The smoothing plane, shorter than a jack plane, is used to achieve a fine, smooth final surface finish.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A long hand plane used to produce a very straight, true edge or surface on timber, especially for jointing longer pieces, is called a
questions.explanation: The trying (jointer) plane's greater length helps produce very straight, true edges and surfaces, ideal for jointing long boards.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A hand plane specifically designed to cut a stepped recess (rebate) along the edge of timber is called a
questions.explanation: A rebate plane is designed to cut a stepped rectangular recess along the edge of a workpiece.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A hand plane specifically designed to cut a groove parallel to the edge of timber, such as for panel joints, is called a
questions.explanation: A plough plane cuts a groove running parallel to the edge of timber, commonly used for grooves that receive panels or tongues.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A small hand tool, held with both hands, used to shape and smooth curved or rounded timber surfaces is called a
questions.explanation: A spoke shave is a small, two-handled tool specifically suited to shaping and smoothing curved surfaces, such as chair spindles.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Sharpening a plane iron or chisel by rubbing its bevel on a coarse grinding wheel to restore its cutting angle is called
questions.explanation: Grinding removes more material to restore the correct bevel angle on a badly worn or damaged cutting edge.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Sharpening a plane iron or chisel by rubbing its bevel on a fine oilstone to produce a keen cutting edge is called
questions.explanation: Honing refines and sharpens the cutting edge on a fine stone, following the coarser grinding process, to achieve a truly keen edge.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A chisel with a flat, relatively thick blade, suitable for general-purpose paring and light chopping work, is called a
questions.explanation: The firmer chisel has a flat, sturdy blade suited for general-purpose chopping and paring tasks.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A chisel with angled edges along its sides, allowing it to access tight corners such as in dovetail joints, is called a
questions.explanation: The bevel-edged chisel's angled sides allow it to reach into tight corners, particularly useful for cleaning out dovetail joints.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A robust, thick-bladed chisel specifically designed to withstand heavy mallet blows when chopping mortises is called a
questions.explanation: The mortise chisel is thick and strong, built to withstand repeated heavy mallet blows when chopping deep mortise recesses.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A chisel with a curved blade, used for cutting hollows or curved profiles in timber, is called a
questions.explanation: A gouge has a curved cutting edge, suited to carving hollows or shaping curved profiles in timber.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A hand tool with a ratcheting mechanism, used with interchangeable bits to bore holes in timber, is called a
questions.explanation: A ratchet brace allows a bit to be turned to bore holes even in confined spaces, using its ratcheting mechanism to work with a limited swing.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A boring bit designed specifically to drill a hole for inserting a cylindrical wooden dowel is called a
questions.explanation: A dowel bit is shaped to bore the precise hole needed to accommodate a cylindrical wooden dowel joint.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A boring bit used to create a shallow, cone-shaped recess so that a screw head sits flush with or below the timber surface is called a
questions.explanation: A countersink bit cuts a conical recess that allows a screw's head to sit flush with, or slightly below, the surrounding surface.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A hammer with a curved, split head used both for driving nails and for extracting them is called a
questions.explanation: A claw hammer combines a flat striking face for driving nails with a curved, split claw for removing them.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A hammer with a distinctive cross-peen head, often used by woodworkers for lighter tack and pin work, is called a
questions.explanation: The Warrington hammer has a wedge-shaped cross-peen, useful for starting small pins and tacks precisely.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A wooden-headed striking tool used to drive chisels or assemble joints without damaging or marking the wood is called a
questions.explanation: A mallet, typically made of wood, provides a softer strike than a metal hammer, protecting chisel handles and joint surfaces from damage.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Trees that grow by adding new wood in annual rings on the outside of existing wood, beneath the bark, are classified as
questions.explanation: Exogenous trees grow outward, adding new layers of wood just beneath the bark each growing season, forming visible annual rings.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Trees that grow by adding new woody tissue scattered throughout their stem, without distinct annual rings, are classified as
questions.explanation: Endogenous trees, such as palms and bamboo, grow with woody tissue distributed throughout the stem rather than in distinct outer rings.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Timber obtained from coniferous, needle-leaved, cone-bearing trees is generally classified as
questions.explanation: Softwoods come from coniferous trees, generally characterised by needle-like leaves and cone-bearing reproduction, though not always softer in actual hardness.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Timber obtained from broad-leaved, flowering trees is generally classified as
questions.explanation: Hardwoods come from broad-leaved, flowering trees, though the botanical classification does not always correspond directly to greater physical hardness.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The soft, central core of a tree trunk, often the oldest and sometimes weakest part, is called the
questions.explanation: The pith is the small, soft central core running along the length of the tree, often the first-formed and weakest wood tissue.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The darker, inner wood surrounding the pith, typically denser and more decay-resistant than the outer wood, is called the
questions.explanation: Heartwood forms the inner, mature wood of the tree, generally darker in colour and more resistant to decay than sapwood.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The lighter-coloured, outer active wood layer surrounding the heartwood, through which sap is conducted, is called the
questions.explanation: Sapwood is the living, functional outer wood layer that conducts sap, generally lighter in colour and less durable than heartwood.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The thin layer of actively dividing cells located just beneath the bark, responsible for the tree's growth in diameter, is called the
questions.explanation: The cambium layer is a thin band of actively dividing cells responsible for producing new wood and bark, increasing the tree's diameter each year.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The layer of living tissue just outside the cambium, responsible for transporting nutrients produced by the leaves, is called the
questions.explanation: The inner bark (phloem) transports nutrients produced through photosynthesis down from the leaves to the rest of the tree.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The tough, protective outer layer of a tree, shielding it from damage, disease, and moisture loss, is called the
questions.explanation: The outer bark is the tree's protective outer covering, shielding it from physical damage, disease, and excessive moisture loss.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The radiating lines visible in a cross-section of some logs, running from the centre outward, used for the storage and lateral movement of food, are called
questions.explanation: Medullary rays are radial structures that store and transport food laterally across the log, sometimes visible as attractive figure in cut timber.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A traditional method of timber conversion that cuts straight through the log in parallel slices, without regard to the direction of the medullary rays, is called
questions.explanation: Through-and-through (plain) sawing produces parallel slices across the log, offering good yield but variable grain patterns.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A timber conversion method that cuts the log so that the medullary rays run roughly perpendicular to the board's face, producing more stable boards, is called
questions.explanation: Quarter (radial) sawing orients cuts so the medullary rays run near-perpendicular to the board face, producing timber that is more dimensionally stable.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A timber conversion method that cuts the log so that the growth rings run roughly parallel (tangential) to the board's face is called
questions.explanation: Tangential sawing cuts boards so that the growth rings run roughly parallel to the wide face, often producing attractive but less stable figure.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Moisture present in the cell cavities of freshly cut (green) timber, which is the first to be lost during seasoning, is called
questions.explanation: Free water occupies the cell cavities of green timber and is removed first during seasoning, before bound water begins to leave the cell walls.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Moisture held within the actual cell walls of timber, whose removal causes the wood to shrink, is called
questions.explanation: Bound water is held within the cell walls themselves; its removal during seasoning causes the characteristic shrinkage of timber.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The moisture content level at which all free water has been removed but the cell walls remain fully saturated with bound water is called the
questions.explanation: The fibre saturation point marks the transition where free water is gone, but cell walls are still fully saturated; further drying below this point causes shrinkage.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A seasoning defect in which a board twists out of a flat plane along its length is called
questions.explanation: Warping (twisting) describes a board that has distorted out of flat along its length, often due to uneven drying.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A seasoning defect in which a board curves along its length, becoming concave or convex from end to end, is called
questions.explanation: Bowing describes a lengthwise curve developing along a board's face, typically from uneven moisture loss.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A seasoning defect in which a board curves across its width, becoming concave or convex from edge to edge, is called
questions.explanation: Cupping describes a board curving across its width, a common defect from uneven drying between the two faces.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A seasoning defect involving small surface cracks that develop along the grain of a board due to rapid or uneven drying is called
questions.explanation: Checking refers to small surface cracks along the grain, often caused by the outer surface drying and shrinking faster than the interior.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A seasoning defect involving a crack that extends completely through the thickness of a board is called
questions.explanation: Splitting describes a crack that has progressed fully through the thickness of a board, a more severe defect than surface checking.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Drying timber slowly using natural atmospheric conditions, without artificial heat, is called
questions.explanation: Air seasoning dries timber using natural atmospheric conditions over an extended period, without the use of artificial heating.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Drying timber more quickly using controlled heat, humidity, and airflow within a specialised chamber is called
questions.explanation: Kiln seasoning uses a controlled chamber with regulated heat, humidity, and airflow to dry timber more quickly and consistently than natural air seasoning.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A fungal decay affecting timber, causing it to become dry, brittle, and crumble into powder, is called
questions.explanation: Dry rot is a fungal decay that leaves affected timber dry, brittle, and prone to crumbling, despite its name being associated with a fungus requiring some moisture to initiate attack.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A fungal decay affecting timber that remains persistently wet, causing softening and darkening of the affected wood, is called
questions.explanation: Wet rot occurs in timber that remains persistently damp, causing the wood to soften, darken, and decay.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Insects that live in colonies and can cause extensive hidden damage to timber structures by consuming cellulose are called
questions.explanation: Termites live in organised colonies and can cause extensive, often hidden, structural damage by consuming the cellulose in timber.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Small insects whose larvae bore into the sapwood of timber, leaving fine, powdery frass and small exit holes, are called
questions.explanation: Powder-post beetle larvae tunnel through sapwood, leaving behind fine powdery dust (frass) and small round exit holes.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A traditional timber preservative derived from coal tar distillation, providing strong protection against decay and insect attack, is called
questions.explanation: Creosote, a tar-oil preservative derived from coal tar distillation, provides strong, long-lasting protection against fungal decay and insect attack.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A timber preservative in which the active chemicals are dissolved and applied in a water-based solution is called a
questions.explanation: Water-borne preservatives dissolve their active protective chemicals in water, offering an alternative to oil-based products like creosote.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A manufactured wood-based board produced by gluing thin layers (veneers) of wood together with grain directions alternating at right angles is called
questions.explanation: Plywood is manufactured from thin veneers glued together with alternating grain direction, increasing overall strength and stability.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A manufactured wood-based board with a core of solid wood strips sandwiched between outer veneers is called
questions.explanation: Blockboard has a core made of solid wood strips, faced on both sides with veneer, combining strength with lighter weight than solid timber.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A manufactured wood-based board produced by compressing wood particles or chips together with a resin binder is called
questions.explanation: Particleboard (chipboard) is formed by compressing wood chips and particles together with a resin binder under heat and pressure.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A manufactured wood-based board produced by breaking down wood fibres and binding them under heat and pressure into a dense, smooth board, is called
questions.explanation: MDF is made from finely broken-down wood fibres bonded under heat and pressure, producing a dense, smooth-surfaced board popular for furniture and mouldings.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A simple joint formed by gluing (and sometimes nailing) two flat pieces of timber edge to edge to increase width is called a
questions.explanation: A butt joint simply joins two flat surfaces together, typically edge-to-edge, relying mainly on glue for strength.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A widening joint in which one board has a projecting tongue that fits into a matching groove on the adjoining board is called a
questions.explanation: Tongued-and-grooved joints interlock a projecting tongue on one board with a matching groove on the next, improving alignment and strength.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A widening joint reinforced with small cylindrical wooden pegs inserted into matching holes in both boards is called a
questions.explanation: Dowelled joints use cylindrical wooden pegs (dowels) inserted into aligned holes, adding strength and alignment to a glued joint.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A strong framing joint in which a projecting tongue (tenon) on one member fits into a matching slot (mortise) on another is called a
questions.explanation: The mortise and tenon joint is a classic, strong framing joint, where a tenon (tongue) fits securely into a matching mortise (slot).

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A framing joint in which each of the two members has an identical open-ended slot cut, allowing the corresponding tenon to slot into it, is called a
questions.explanation: The bridle joint is a variant of the mortise and tenon joint, featuring a wider open-ended slot into which the matching member fits.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A framing joint formed by removing half the thickness from each of two overlapping members so they fit flush together is called a
questions.explanation: A halving joint removes half the material thickness from each overlapping piece, allowing them to sit flush when joined.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A strong box/carcass joint using interlocking, angled, fan-shaped projections that resist being pulled apart is called a
questions.explanation: Dovetail joints use angled, interlocking projections (pins and tails) that mechanically resist being pulled apart, making them ideal for drawers and boxes.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A box/carcass joint in which a groove is cut across one member to receive the full end of another member is called a
questions.explanation: A housing joint cuts a groove across one member into which the end of another piece fits, commonly used for shelves fitted into cabinet sides.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A traditional adhesive made from animal by-products, historically used in furniture making before synthetic alternatives, is called
questions.explanation: Animal (hide) glue, derived from animal collagen, was a traditional woodworking adhesive widely used before synthetic glues became common.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A synthetic resin adhesive that cures through a chemical reaction, commonly used in the manufacture of plywood and other engineered boards, is called
questions.explanation: Urea-formaldehyde resin is a synthetic adhesive widely used in manufacturing plywood and other engineered wood products.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A common white, water-based synthetic adhesive widely used for general woodworking and joinery is called
questions.explanation: PVA glue is a widely used, easy-to-apply, water-based adhesive suitable for most general woodworking applications.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: An adhesive applied to both surfaces and allowed to dry before pressing together, forming an immediate strong bond on contact, is called
questions.explanation: Contact cement is applied to both surfaces and allowed to become tacky before joining, bonding immediately and strongly upon contact.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Metal fasteners such as nails, screws, and dowels, along with hardware like hinges, locks, and catches, are collectively used in woodwork mainly to
options: measure and mark out timber accurately
join and secure components together, and to add functional hardware to finished pieces
finish and decorate the surface of timber
questions.explanation: Fasteners and hardware provide mechanical joining and functional features (like opening doors or locking drawers) in completed woodwork projects.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The process of removing surface irregularities from timber using progressively finer abrasive papers before finishing is called
questions.explanation: Sanding with progressively finer grits smooths the timber surface, preparing it for stains, fillers, or a final finish.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A finishing material used to colour timber while allowing its natural grain pattern to remain visible is called a
questions.explanation: Stains add colour to timber while allowing the natural wood grain to show through, unlike opaque paint.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A finishing material used to fill the natural open pores of certain timbers, providing a smoother base before applying a top coat, is called a
questions.explanation: Fillers close the open pores of coarse-grained timbers, creating a smoother surface ready for the final finishing coats.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A traditional, highly glossy finish built up from many thin coats of shellac applied with a rubbing pad is called
questions.explanation: French polish is a traditional shellac-based finish, built up in many thin layers using a rubbing pad, producing a deep, glossy shine.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A clear or tinted protective finish, typically applied by brush, that dries to form a hard, glossy or satin surface film is called
questions.explanation: Varnish forms a hard, protective, glossy or satin film over timber, protecting it while allowing the wood's appearance to show through if clear.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A fast-drying clear or tinted finish, often applied by spraying, that forms a protective film through solvent evaporation is called a
questions.explanation: Lacquer dries quickly as its solvents evaporate, commonly applied by spraying to produce a hard, protective clear or tinted finish.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: An opaque finishing material that completely covers and colours the surface of timber, hiding the natural wood grain, is called
questions.explanation: Paint provides an opaque coating that fully covers the timber surface, hiding the natural grain, unlike stains or clear varnishes.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: When applying finishing materials such as lacquers and varnishes, an important safety precaution is to
options: ensure adequate ventilation, since many finishes release flammable or harmful fumes
apply the finish in a sealed room with no ventilation
avoid reading the manufacturer's safety instructions
smoke or use open flames nearby for convenience
questions.explanation: Many wood finishes release flammable or harmful solvent fumes, making good ventilation an essential safety precaution during application.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A through dovetail joint, visible from both faces of the joined boards, is commonly used mainly for
options: widening narrow boards edge to edge
carcass and box corners where strength and visible craftsmanship are both valued
temporary joints intended to be dismantled easily
questions.explanation: Through dovetails are visible on both faces of a joint and are commonly used at box and carcass corners, valued for their strength and craftsmanship.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A lapped dovetail joint, in which the joint is hidden from one face, is often chosen over a through dovetail mainly for
options: drawer fronts, where a neat, unbroken outer appearance is desired
questions.explanation: Lapped dovetails conceal the joint from the front face, making them a popular choice for drawer fronts where an unbroken, neat appearance is desired.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: The angled projections on a dovetail joint that resemble a dove's spread tail are specifically called the
questions.explanation: A dovetail joint's interlocking angled projections are known as tails (wider) and pins (narrower), together forming the joint.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A stopped housing joint, in which the groove does not run the full width of the receiving member, is used mainly to
options: increase the overall joint's structural strength beyond a through housing
allow the joint to be assembled without any fitting
eliminate the need for glue entirely
hide the joint from the front edge, improving the finished appearance
questions.explanation: A stopped housing joint conceals the groove from the front edge of the piece, improving the visual appearance of the finished item compared to a through housing.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A haunched mortise and tenon joint includes a small additional shoulder (haunch) mainly to
options: eliminate the need for a mortise altogether
reduce the overall strength of the joint intentionally
fill the remaining groove space and add resistance against twisting at corner joints
allow the joint to be used only for widening boards
questions.explanation: The haunch fills the space left when a tenon meets a grooved frame member, and helps resist twisting, particularly useful at corner joints like door frames.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Cramping (clamping) a glued joint firmly while the adhesive cures is important mainly to
options: prevent the timber from seasoning further
ensure close contact between surfaces for a strong, even bond
speed up the chemical curing process itself
replace the need for accurate joint-cutting
questions.explanation: Clamping holds glued surfaces in firm, even contact while the adhesive cures, which is essential for achieving a strong, well-bonded joint.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A key consideration when selecting an appropriate joint for a piece of furniture is
options: the type and direction of stress the joint will need to resist in use
the colour of the timber being used
the brand of glue available in the workshop
the total number of tools owned by the maker
questions.explanation: Joint selection should be guided by the forces the finished piece will experience in use, ensuring the chosen joint provides adequate strength in the right directions.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Wood screws are generally preferred over nails in furniture joinery when
options: the timber is extremely thin and easily split
the fastest possible assembly with no future disassembly is needed
greater holding power and the ability to disassemble the joint later are required
the joint will never experience any load
questions.explanation: Screws provide stronger holding power than nails and allow for later disassembly, making them preferable for many furniture applications.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Pre-drilling (boring a pilot hole) before driving a screw into timber helps mainly to
options: change the timber's natural grain direction
increase the total holding power beyond a properly sized screw
prevent the timber from splitting and make driving the screw easier
eliminate the need for any adhesive
questions.explanation: Pre-drilling a pilot hole reduces the risk of splitting the timber and makes it considerably easier to drive the screw straight and true.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: Hinges, locks, and catches used on furniture and joinery items are collectively referred to as
questions.explanation: Ironmongery refers to the metal hardware fittings, such as hinges, locks, and catches, used to complete functional furniture and joinery items.

questions.subject: Woodwork
questions.text: A working drawing for a piece of furniture typically shows
options: only a general artistic impression with no measurements
the dimensions, joints, and construction details needed to build the item accurately
the history of the furniture style only
questions.explanation: A working drawing provides the precise dimensions, joint details, and construction information a craftsman needs to accurately build a piece of furniture.
